title: The ninety-nine
tomorrow: the waiting room. what do you pray when you don't know what to ask?

cards: Three in the morning, the night before a surgery. A teenager comes downstairs for water and stops in the doorway. The kitchen light is on.
Her grandmother sits at the table in her shawl, a string of prayer beads moving through her fingers, lips moving. Not a list of requests. Just a word, over and over, under her breath.
Ya Latif. Ya Latif. The girl sits down across from her and asks: what are you asking for?
And her grandmother says: I'm not asking for anything yet. I'm calling Him by His name.

teach.b: Ya Latif: O Gentle One, the One who reaches into the smallest places.
It's one of God's names, and a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says there are ninety-nine of them, a hundred minus one, and whoever learns them by heart and lives by them enters the garden.

The Qur'an puts it simply, in Pickthall's words: "Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them." Elsewhere it says: call on Allah or call on the Merciful, by whichever name you call, the most beautiful names are His.
So the names aren't a password.

teach.h: THE NAME THAT FITS THE MOMENT.
teach.b: They're a way of calling the One who fits the moment.
Afraid, people call As-Salam, Peace. Lonely, Al-Wadud, the Loving. Ashamed, Al-Ghafur, the Forgiving.
Sick, the Prophet ﷺ himself prayed over the ill by calling God the Healer, and said there's no healing but His.
And the grandmother at three a.m. calls the Gentle One, because tomorrow a surgeon's hands will need gentleness, and so will she.

Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the last verses of the Qur'an's fifty-ninth surah, al-Hashr, read like a necklace of names strung one after another: the King, the Holy One, Peace, the Faithful, the Guardian, and on.
A whole necklace. At three in the morning, the grandmother needed only one bead of it.

how: Muslims call on God by His names in du'a and dhikr, often counting them on prayer beads, and many learn the ninety-nine names by heart, sometimes as a song in weekend school.

games.q: a friend wants to pray before a hard exam, but says she doesn't know 'the right words.' what fits today?
o: call God by a name that fits what she needs, in her own words.
wait until she has learned all ninety-nine names in Arabic.
use only the name Allah; the other names are for scholars.
games.why: 'invoke Him by them' (7:180), and 'by whichever name you call' (17:110). the names are doors, not a test.

practice: Open your hands, palms up, the way people hold them in du'a. Call on three names slowly, with a few breaths between: Ar-Rahman, the Merciful; As-Salam, Peace; Al-Latif, the Gentle.
Without words, open hands work too: let each meaning settle on its own.

wordCard.voice: The ninety-nine: God's most beautiful names, a hundred minus one, each a way to call on Him.

orig.note: Arabic: the most beautiful names, God's names in the Qur'an and hadith.

carryVoice: Keep this: call him by his names, the one that fits the night you're in. Ten of fifteen.
